title: Diffuse leukoencephalopathy in a 29-year-old male with hypertensive emergency
case_prompt:
A 29-year-old man was referred to the emergency department by his ophthalmologist after a blood pressure measurement of 250/150 mmHg and findings of retinal hemorrhages. He reported a 2-week history of blurred vision, a 2-month history of headache, and several days of unsteady gait. Family members noted recent confusion. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, arthralgias, urinary symptoms, smoking, illicit drug use, and over-the-counter intake except occasional ibuprofen. He had previously consumed alcohol heavily but had reduced intake 2 weeks earlier. He had no significant past medical history and no features of Cushing syndrome. On examination, his blood pressure was 250/150 mmHg, and an S4 gallop was auscultated. Neurologic exam was notable only for visual disturbance.

Laboratory studies showed creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, bicarbonate 21 mEq/L, chloride 109 mEq/L, hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL dropping to 10.5 g/dL the next day, indirect bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL (normal <0.5 mg/dL), lactate dehydrogenase 352 U/L, and low haptoglobin. A peripheral smear was negative for schistocytes. Repeat LDH and creatinine began to improve.

Brain MRI revealed extensive bilateral supratentorial and infratentorial subcortical hyperintensities involving the splenium of the corpus callosum and pons, with sparing of subcortical U-fibers and two foci of petechial hemorrhage in the cerebellum. There was no evidence of restricted diffusion or post-contrast enhancement. MR angiography was unremarkable.

Further evaluation included a negative urine drug screen; negative serologies for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil-cytoplasmic antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and normal complement fixation tests; an aldosterone-to-renin ratio < 20; and mildly elevated catecholamine levels in the context of clonidine therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Secondary hypertension (e.g., hyperaldosteronism) was considered — “His aldosterone to renin ratio was < 20.”  
2. Vasculitis was considered — “Serological evaluation (antinuclear antibodies, anti-neutrophil-cytoplasmic antibodies and rheumatoid factor) was negative and his complement fixation tests were normal.”  
3. Drug toxicity was considered — “A drug screen was performed on the patient and was negative.”  
4. Pheochromocytoma was considered — “His catecholamine levels were mildly elevated but the patient was on clonidine.”  
5. Subarachnoid haemorrhage and acute stroke were considered — “No evidence of restricted diffusion or post-contrast enhancement was seen.”  
6. Hepatic and uremic encephalopathy were considered — “His creatinine level of 1.6 mg dl −1 and blood urea nitrogen of 18 mg dl −1. His indirect bilirubin level was elevated at 0.9 mg dl −1 (normal < 0.5 mg dl −1 ).”  
7. Eclampsia and pre-eclampsia were considered — “The differential diagnoses of hypertension and encephalopathy include … eclampsia and pre-eclampsia in females …”
